# A Forecasting Pipeline

Build a pipeline that forecasts a numeric time series (river level for the
disaster example, or population counts for the ecology example) by fitting a
simple trend and seasonal model, and judge it by forecasting the held-out
recent past. A distinct kind of analysis: prediction over time.

-   A forecast is an extrapolation, and its error grows with the horizon.
-   Naive and seasonal baselines give a floor to beat.
-   Backtesting holds out the recent past to judge a model.
-   Forecast uncertainty matters as much as the point forecast.

## A synthetic river series

-   We need a series whose shape we control, so we generate one: a slow rising
    trend plus a yearly cycle plus random noise.
-   The disaster example forecasts `river_level` from the `readings` series;
    the ecology example forecasts population `count` from the `environment`
    series, and the same code runs with the column renamed.
-   Pin the seed first so the series is reproducible.

{{< inc forecasting/forecasting.py mark=setup >}}

-   A monthly reading over six years gives 72 points.
-   The level is a base height plus a trend that rises a little each month, a
    sine wave that repeats every 12 months, and Gaussian noise.
-   The sine wave is the season: winter highs and summer lows, or any repeating
    yearly pattern.

{{< inc forecasting/forecasting.py mark=generate >}}

-   `t` is the month index; the level is everything else.

## Hold out the recent past

-   Backtesting means pretending the last stretch of the series has not
    happened yet: we fit only on the earlier points and forecast the rest.
-   The held-out points are the recent past, and they are the honest test: the
    model never sees them while it is being fit.
-   We hold out the final year.

{{< inc forecasting/forecasting.py mark=split >}}

## A naive baseline

-   The simplest forecast repeats the last known value for every future point.
-   It is nearly always wrong, but it gives a floor: a real model should beat
    it, or the model is not earning its keep.

{{< inc forecasting/forecasting.py mark=baseline >}}

## A trend and seasonal model

-   A slightly smarter model fits a straight line through the series to capture
    the trend.
-   The slope is the average change per month, estimated by least squares; the
    intercept is where that line starts.

{{< inc forecasting/forecasting.py mark=trend >}}

-   After removing the trend, what is left is the seasonal shape plus noise.
-   Average the detrended leftovers by month: month 0 gets the mean of every
    January leftover, month 1 the mean of every February, and so on.
-   Those twelve averages are the additive seasonal terms.
-   The spread of the residuals around the fitted pattern, `sigma`, is our
    first estimate of the typical error.

{{< inc forecasting/forecasting.py mark=seasonal >}}

-   Forecasting is just extending the line: for each month ahead, add the trend
    times that month plus that month's seasonal term.

{{< inc forecasting/forecasting.py mark=forecast >}}

## Measure the error

-   Mean absolute error is the average distance between the forecast and the
    truth, in the units of the series.
-   We compute it on the held-out points, which the fit never saw.

{{< inc forecasting/forecasting.py mark=evaluate >}}

-   The trend and seasonal model should beat the naive baseline, because it
    captures the yearly rise and fall that the naive forecast ignores.
-   Beating the naive floor is the minimum bar; it does not mean the forecast
    is good.

## Plot actual vs forecast

-   Altair draws the actual held-out points and both forecasts on the same
    axes.
-   The closer a forecast line sits to the actual line, the smaller its error.

{{< inc forecasting/forecasting.py mark=plot >}}

-   The naive line is flat, so it misses the seasonal curve entirely.
-   The trend+seasonal line bends with the season, so it tracks the actual
    values much more closely.

## Forecast uncertainty

-   A point forecast is a single number; a useful forecast also says how sure
    we are.
-   `sigma` from the training fit is a first estimate of the typical error.
-   A rough interval is the forecast plus or minus two sigma: about 95% of
    values should land inside if the errors are normal and independent.

{{< inc forecasting/forecasting.py mark=uncertainty >}}

-   The interval widens as we forecast further ahead, because each step adds
    new uncertainty.
-   For the naive model the error accumulates like a random walk, so its
    interval grows with the square root of the horizon.
-   A constant band is a simplification; a real pipeline reports a band that
    widens with the horizon.

-   The ecology twin forecasts population `count` the same way: generate a
    trend plus seasonal series, hold out the recent past, fit the naive and
    trend+seasonal models, and compare their MAE.
-   Rename the column and adjust the units, and the pipeline runs unchanged.
